name: Bura-Pabir
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Hoffmann, Carl. 1955. Untersuchungen zur Struktur und sprachlichen Stellung des Bura (grammar); Olalekan 2011, Aspects of Bura phonology.
earlier_scan.note: Multiple grammars/phonologies of Bura exist but none fetchable (Hoffmann print-only; afribary thesis copy 403); language is tonal per Badejo 1989.

new_statements.quote: Like most Nigerian languages, Bura is a tone language. Its tone system is yet to be fully worked out. Davies (1954-56) pointed to a three-way tone contrast as follows; ká swear / ka and, with / kà let, may … Almost certainly, however, Bura has two tones and downstep. Downstep is a tone which sounds like high tone but which has the effect of lowering the tones of the rest of the sentence. Such systems are very common in Chadic languages. [...] Bura has phonetic rising tone caused by sequences of two vowels with different tones. [...] However, it seems to have rare phonemic rising tone.
new_statements.citation: Blench, Roger. 2009. Bura phonology and some suggestions concerning the orthography. Draft circulated for comment, printout 10 July 2009. Cambridge: Kay Williamson Educational Foundation. 9 pp.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened says anything about word stress or accent. The only prosodic statement is that Bura is a tone language with (probably) two lexical tones H and L plus downstep, rare phonemic rising tone, and phonetic rises across vowel sequences (Blench 2009). Schuh's 1981-82 wordlist marks lexical tone on every headword (H, L, falling on some, e.g. tlâata), corroborating lexical tone contrast; Blench's 2010 dictionary draft marks tone only sporadically and leaves its 'Phonology' heading empty. The mission grammar notes (Bura Grammar for a Beginner) mention tone only once (possessive pronoun constructions).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: Davies (1954-56, the 'Biu Book') posited a three-way tone contrast which Blench reinterprets as two tones plus downstep; tone marking is described as unsettled ('yet to be fully worked out').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone (minimal sets ká/ka/kà; dictionary headwords). Blench 2009 is a circulated draft, not a peer-reviewed publication, based on a 2009 Jos lexicography workshop and mission materials from the Garkida area; Maddieson 1983 and Schuh's list are based on a single Garkida speaker (Elisha Shalanguwa). None of the opened sources treats Pabir separately.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened materials describe Bura proper (Garkida / Biu-area mission variety; Schuh's and Maddieson's data from one Garkida speaker, Elisha Shalanguwa; Blench's from the 2009 Jos workshop with the Bura Literacy Committee). Glottolog bura1292 'Bura-Pabir' also covers Pabir (Babur); no opened source treats Pabir separately or gives it a distinct prosody. No dialect-level glottocode applies.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger (ed.). 2010. A Dictionary of Bura [draft printout 25 July 2010], based on the 1950s Garkida mission mimeo (O. Shankster), Schuh's wordlist and Blench fieldnotes. Cambridge: KWEF. 201 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. §2 'Phonology' is an empty heading; front matter says 'Tone is only sporadically marked... No Bura speakers have yet been trained to mark tone accurately' (p. ii); §5 orthography issues concerns consonant/vowel letters only.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. with Elisha Shalanguwa. 2010 [data 1981-82]. Bura-English-Hausa Dictionary. Unpublished ms., Los Angeles (Unicode export 17 Aug 2010), c. 1500-1600 tone-marked headwords.
sources.note: Introduction covers orthography and the two classes of word-final vowels (stable vs. deleted/reduced to schwa phrase-medially); headwords carry tone marks (H, L, falling), but there is no statement on stress or on the tone system.

sources.citation: [Church of the Brethren missionaries]; Balami, Moses & Helen Butler (eds.); Roger Blench (2009 Unicode ed.). 2009 [2004]. Bura Grammar for a Beginner. Bura Language and Bible Translation Project. 47 pp. (Glottolog 87399/153953)
sources.note: Pedagogical grammar notes with no pronunciation/phonology chapter; only prosodic remark is 'Tone is important where the possessor is a pronoun' (p. 5). Nothing on word stress.

sources.citation: Maddieson, Ian. 1983. The analysis of complex phonetic elements in Bura and the syllable. Studies in African Linguistics 14(3): 285-310.
sources.note: Instrumental study of the 'labial-alveolar' consonants and syllabification (one Garkida speaker); the only prosodic mention is a rule deleting 'a short high low-toned vowel' (p. 300); silent on stress.

sources.citation: Malgwi Yunana, Inuwa. 2018. A critical analysis of the sound system of the Bura language by a mother tongue speaker. MA thesis, University of Jos. 77 pp. (Glottolog 557953)
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Most recent phonological description, by a native speaker; would confirm the two-tone-plus-downstep analysis and state whether stress plays any role; Glottolog/hh holds the PDF.

sources.citation: Olalekan, Oluwaseun Paul. 2011. Aspects of Bura phonology. MA thesis, Department of Linguistics and Nigerian Languages, University of Ilorin. 88 pp. (Glottolog 551235)
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Only modern monograph-length phonology of Bura; Nigerian MA phonologies of this type routinely have a 'suprasegmentals' chapter treating tone and stress explicitly. Glottolog's hh bibliography holds the PDF ('delivered'), so a copy exists in the Hammarström collection.

sources.citation: Badejo, B. Rotimi. 1989. An experimental study of tone-marking in Bura. Frankfurter Afrikanistische Blätter 1: 44-51. (Glottolog 77798)

sources.note: The only instrumental prosodic study of Bura; would settle the number of tones (Davies' three vs. Blench's two + downstep) and may comment on intensity/prominence.
